summary: Globes article by Assaf Gilead arguing that Israel's over-reliance on technology (the Gaza barrier, sensors, Iron Dome, visual intelligence) and a 'small and smart army' concept left it exposed to Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack. Experts such as Avner Barnea, Eviatar Matania, Eran Ortal and Giora Eiland argue that technology has vulnerabilities and needs redundancy, that it fostered a policy of restraint, and that spotting strategic surprises is a human process based on 'weak signals' and scenario thinking.
one_line: Experts argue Israel's faith in high-tech border defenses, Iron Dome and visual intelligence set the stage for the October 7 strategic surprise.
key_facts: The Gaza border barrier was completed in December 2021, cost NIS 3.5 billion (mostly for the below-ground section), and relied mainly on sensors, cameras and vehicle patrols with almost no soldiers.
The decision to build the 'anti-tunnel barrier' was made in 2016 after Operation Protective Edge in 2014 showed Hamas could penetrate border settlements via tunnels.
On October 7, Hamas used cheaply bought drones to disable the cameras and the (See and Fire) remote controlled weapon stations (RCWS) on the Gaza barrier.
The three observation balloons had stopped working some weeks before the attack, and repairs were postponed until 'after the holidays.'
The IDF's Iron Beam high energy laser interception system had not yet entered operational activity after many years of development.
According to The New York Times, the IDF stopped monitoring Hamas' radio communications a year before the attack.
Eviatar Matania says IDF senior officers often see technological systems as 'black boxes' and that systems need redundancy so there is no single point of vulnerability.
Brig. Gen. Eran Ortal wrote in 2018 that Iron Dome and the barrier helped produce a policy of restraint toward Gaza, which let Hamas build offensive capabilities.
Ortal said that even Iron Dome's complete success left daily life on the home front in the hands of terrorist organizations, citing imperfection, enormous cost, and sirens and shelters.
Avner Barnea says a study of intelligence failures from 1989 to 2010 showed no improvement in warning of strategic surprises despite better information-gathering means.
On the day of the attack, suspicious movement in Gaza led the Shin Bet head to send a special team south, but he could not persuade top IDF echelons to prepare accordingly.
Giora Eiland argues for 'scenario theory': prepare for low-probability, devastating scenarios, since preparation like waking troops at 4:00 am and launching unmanned aircraft is cheap.
Eiland had lectured senior officers in the months before October 7 on the strategic surprise of the Yom Kippur War.
